sentences.text: There is only one accepted species, Anchiornis huxleyi, a small bipedal theropod with a triangular skull that shares traits with dromaeosaurids, troodontids, and early birds.
This creature was roughly the size of a crow, possessing forelimbs that measured eighty percent of the total length of its hindlimbs.
Its wings held between twenty and twenty-eight primary feathers, which featured curved, symmetrical quills with rounded tips indicating limited aerodynamic ability.
Long, vaned feathers covered its hind legs, leading some researchers to propose it was a four-winged dinosaur where these structures served for display rather than flight.
Anchiornis holds the distinction of being the earliest known theropod to produce gastric pellets, with some preserved inside the fossilized bodies.
Scientists mapped its coloration using melanosomes, revealing a complex pattern of speckles across the body and wings likely used for communication.
The genus was formally described by Xu Xing and his colleagues in the year 2009.
The type specimen, catalogued as IVPP V14378, was discovered in the Yaolugou area of Jianchang County, Liaoning, China.
Fossils of this animal have been found exclusively within the Tiaojishan Formation, with three recorded occurrences listed in the Paleobiology Database.
A 2016 study suggested juveniles might use wings to assist running up inclines, while adults likely lacked a bony breastbone, possibly having one made of cartilage instead.
The hind wing structures were likely used mainly for display rather than flight, given their smaller size and symmetrical feathers.
Researchers initially speculated that Anchiornis could fly or glide, but later studies suggested it was likely flightless due to heavy body weight relative to wing area.
Avialans are more closely related to modern birds than to dromaeosaurid and troodontid dinosaurs.
A 2017 re-evaluation placed Anchiornis in the family Anchiornithidae alongside genera like Eosinopteryx and Xiaotingia.
However, the Paleobiology Database lists Troodontidae as the parent group and classifies Anchiornis within the family Troodontidae.
Anchiornis fossils date to the Late Jurassic, specifically the Oxfordian period, when the animal lived approximately 160 million years ago.
Most studies date the rocks containing Anchiornis to between 160.89 and 160.25 million years ago.
Other dating methods place its existence between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago during the Bathonian to Kimmeridgian stages.

The status of Aurornis xui, Eosinopteryx brevipenna, and Serikornis sungei as synonyms of Anchiornis is questioned, with Hu Dongyu and colleagues reclassifying Anchiornis as a troodontid based on features in a second specimen, while Li et al. interpreted Eosinopteryx brevipenna as a junior synonym of Anchiornis huxleyi.
